name: Newberry & Dole's Forwarding and Commission Warehouse
aka: Newberry and Dole's Forwarding and Commission House

placement.symbolic_location: South bank of the main stem, on the South Water Street river frontage west of the built-up blocks, with its dock on the water. THE BANK IS DISPUTED — see the note; the north bank is the other reading and is not adopted here.

construction.note: 'a square FRAME building' in the c. 1835 views reported by docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.10. The dossier tags that [DOC] and names no source record, so this project cannot cite it and carries the reading as inference until the view is identified. `light_frame` is the archetype's term for boards laid horizontally on a stick frame, which is what a frame building looks like at this level of detail; what is behind the boards is not visible and is not claimed.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 3.4 m is about 11 ft at the eave — a tall single storey with storage in the roof, which is the working arrangement of a forwarding and commission house: goods in at ground level off the dock, stored above. Stated rather than left to the archetype's size-aware default of 4.1 m for a footprint this size, which would read as a full two storeys and would be a claim. The firm's LATER warehouse is described hoisting wheat 'to the upper story by Irish power, with rope and pully' (Andreas scan p. 1139) — that is the 1839 building, so it supports the practice and says nothing about this one.

door.note: No source describes an opening. 'wagon' is the archetype's widest doorway, a clear 2.9 m for a loaded team, and it is what a forwarding and commission business needs: the whole trade is taking goods off wagons and boats and putting them back on. A narrower door would say the house was a shop.

loft.note: Not attested for this building. A forwarding warehouse stores above the floor it loads on, and the archetype builds exactly one external trace of that — the door goods are hoisted through, high in a gable end — and nothing else: no dormer, no floor line, no second range of windows. Andreas's description of the firm's 1839 warehouse hoisting wheat to the upper storey is the practice this infers from, four years the wrong side of the scene date.

dock.note: STATED AND NOT BUILT. The dossier's phrase for both river warehouses is 'each had a warehouse with its dock along the river front' (docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.10), and Andreas independently names 'Newberry & Dole's wharf' as the place the schooner Illinois was cheered on 12 July 1834 (scan p. 503). So a dock is well supported and NONE OF IT REACHES THE MESH: this project has a pier_crib archetype for the harbour piers and nothing for a river-front wharf, and inventing one here would put a structure of unknown length, height and construction in the water on the strength of a preposition. The record therefore shows a warehouse standing back from a bare bank, which understates the site — the dock is the half of it that made the building worth building. Owed an admission in docs/LIBERTIES.md.

function.note: 'NEWBERRY & DOLE, Forwarding & Commission MERCHANTS' — the firm's own paid advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, the first contemporary document in this dataset and about as good as evidence of a trade gets, since the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him. Andreas's summary of the paper's advertising columns lists the same firm in the same words (scan p. 755). Forwarding and commission is the lake trade: taking goods off vessels, holding them, and sending them on inland, on commission. The firm's wharf received the schooner Illinois, the first vessel through the new harbour cut, on 12 July 1834 (Andreas scan p. 503).

occupants.value: Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole
occupants.note: The partners are named together in the Democrat's advertisement and repeatedly in Andreas, who gives both first names in the packing-house chapter — 'Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole' (scan p. 1151). The value records whose business it was, not who was on the premises on any day.

citations.citation: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time. Vol. 1. Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884.
The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday, November 26, 1833.

research_note: THIS RECORD EXISTS TO CARRY A DISAGREEMENT, NOT TO END ONE, AND THE POSITION NOTE IS WHERE THE DISAGREEMENT LIVES. Two of this project's own dossiers put Newberry & Dole's warehouse on opposite banks of the Chicago River and one of them says in as many words 'Do not put it on South Water Street'. The building is placed on the south bank, the position is tagged conjectural, and the reasoning is written out with both citations so a later reader can overturn it on the evidence rather than on the shape of the file. THE ONE THING THAT MOVED THE ARGUMENT IN THIS SLICE was reading Andreas's north-bank sentence in place: it sits inside an account of a grain shipment made in 1839 on the brig Osceola, so the warehouse it locates is the firm's warehouse four years after the scene date. That does not make the south bank right; it makes the north-bank citation the wrong date rather than the wrong place. THREE BUILDINGS MUST BE KEPT APART and this dataset now holds all three: dole_warehouse_south, George W. Dole's 1832 warehouse and slaughter yard near the later Tremont House site; newberry_dole_slaughterhouse_south_branch, the firm's 1834 killing and packing plant; and this one, the forwarding and commission house on the river. A fourth — the 1838-39 grain warehouse and elevator on the north bank east of Rush Street, the one that made Chicago's first grain shipments — is LATER THAN THE SCENE and must not be modelled; it is the building Andreas's north-bank sentence describes. WHAT WOULD RESOLVE THE BANK: identifying the c. 1835 view the dossier reports and giving it a source record; or any Chicago Democrat advertisement of 1834-35 carrying the firm's street address, which is exactly the kind of evidence the paper's advertising columns supply and exactly the reason more of the paper should be read into this dataset.
